items.text: SEASON 11 · EPISODE 4 · DRAFT · CASE-058  The Brennock County EOC briefing room · the second storm · Maya, Imogen (public information officer), Amara (accessibility lead) and Director Oduya · Level L6 · Mastery support (reference only — choose the tool and say why)  The warning said “move to higher ground now.” The county said “stay alert.” A family at a low-water crossing believed the county.  ⚑ RV-184: warnings are relayed verbatim; only the director orders evacuations; nothing here tells you how to act in a real emergency — follow your local officials. RV-182: who owns what. Some choices run on a clock — and some depend on your loadout.

items.title: Verbatim
items.stakes: A flash flood warning went out softer than it was issued — in two languages — and a family waited at a crossing.
items.clock: Before the next warning — any minute.
items.reward: Every warning in its owner's words, in every language, in under a minute.

objectives.text: Decide what to do right now
Decide how every language gets them

items.rumor: You are a wire, not an editor.

items.alt: The briefing room, the stream live; Imogen, the public information officer, holds the printed warning; Maya holds the county's post on a tablet.

bubbles.text: I didn't want people to panic. ‘Protect your life’ sounds like the end of the world.
It was meant to. That's the agency's call, not ours.

items.text: Act I — “Seven minutes and different words”

items.prompt: 16:26. The county's post softened a flash flood warning. The storm isn't over. What now?

hints.text: Whose words are they — and who can put them right in a minute?

options.label: Edit the county's post yourself to the agency's words
options.result: Imogen: “Those are the county's channels. Tell me.”
options.consequence: The right words through the wrong hands.
options.fail: The county's channels are the PIO's, with the director.

options.label: Tell Imogen and Director Oduya now: correct it to the agency's words, verbatim and attributed; the director decides what the county adds
options.result: Corrected at 16:27. Oduya adds, separately: ‘County: Mill Creek crossing closed.’
options.consequence: Fix the words through their owners, in a minute.

options.label: Post ‘EVACUATE MILL CREEK NOW’ to make up for it
options.consequence: Overcorrects with an order that isn't yours.
options.fail: Evacuations come only from the director (RV-184).

options.label: Leave it — the agency's own alert reached phones anyway
options.result: Half the valley follows the county's channels, not the agency's.

items.title: Seven minutes and different words.
items.body: The relay log tells it: the agency's warning arrived at 16:12:05. Imogen drafted a softer version, the approval took two more minutes, and it posted at 16:19:00; captions followed six seconds later. Four hundred and fifteen seconds — and the only step that changed the meaning was the first one. A verbatim relay would have taken under a minute.
items.label: Test: where did the minutes go — and where did the words change?

items.sub: Mastery · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Imogen and Maya beside a board. The warning said ‘move to higher ground now’. I wrote ‘flooding possible, stay alert’. I didn't want people panicking. It went out seven minutes after the agency's, in different words — and then into Spanish. Where does the time go?

items.title: 16:12:05 in · 16:19:00 out
items.body: The alert relay's log: ‘16:12:05 received (agency feed) · 16:14:10 draft saved (PIO) · 16:17:02 approved · 16:19:00 published · 16:19:06 captions.’ Five minutes of the seven were the rewrite.

items.prompt: How should warnings flow from now on?
items.risk: The next warning changed the same way.
timeout: The next warning goes through the same rewrite.

options.label: The PIO rewrites every warning in plain language
options.result: Every warning becomes the county's interpretation of it.

options.label: The relay inserts the agency's text verbatim with its name and time; the county's guidance goes out as a separate, labelled message; evacuation wording only from the director
options.result: Imogen reads it twice: “That's what I needed. I never wanted to write their words.”
options.consequence: Verbatim by design, and the county's voice kept for the county's words.

options.label: Relay everything automatically with no human in the loop
options.result: Fast — and the county's closures and shelters never go out.
options.consequence: Solves the rewrite and loses the county's voice.

options.label: Relay only after the director has read each warning
options.result: Every warning waits for one person in a flood.
options.consequence: A bottleneck between the agency and the public.

items.title: The warning nobody believed
items.body: On 31 May 1889, as rain swelled the lake behind the South Fork dam above Johnstown, Pennsylvania, warnings were telegraphed down the valley that the dam might fail. The town had heard warnings like them before, in other springs, and many people stayed. The dam failed that afternoon, and more than two thousand people died. A warning is only as good as the trust in its words.

items.title: The translation.
items.body: Amara pulls up the Spanish post: ‘Posible inundación en Mill Creek. Manténgase alerta.’ Machine-translated — from the rewrite. The captions, too, carried the rewrite word for word. In the shared drive there's a folder for approved warning templates in Spanish, made three years ago. It's empty.
items.label: Test: how many templates — and whose are they?

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #105 · AVERY'S LENS  A warning is relayed in its owner's words  Official warnings travel word for word, attributed and timed; the county adds its own guidance separately — in every language, from text approved before the storm.  A flash flood warning that said ‘move to higher ground now’ was relayed as ‘flooding possible, stay alert’ — and translated from the rewrite.

items.alt: The briefing room; Amara, the accessibility lead, in purple with glasses, points at the caption monitor above head height; Maya reads the Spanish post.

bubbles.text: The people who most needed the real words got a translation of the wrong ones.
Then the real words have to exist in Spanish before the next storm.

items.prompt: So what's left for me, if I can't choose the words?

options.label: “Everything that's the county's: what's closed, where the shelters are, what we're doing. Your voice — just not in their warning.”
options.reply: Separate message. My name on mine, theirs on theirs. I can do that.

options.label: “Nothing, during a warning.”
options.reply: That's not true, and you know it.

options.label: “Ask the director.”
options.reply: I did. She said ask you what's possible.

items.prompt: How does every language — and the captions — carry the warning next time?
items.happening: Spanish and captions carried the rewrite.
unknown: How quickly templates can be approved
items.risk: The people who most need the words getting the wrong ones.
timeout: The next Spanish warning is translated in the moment.

hints.text: What has to exist before the storm so nobody translates in the moment?

items.note: Draft decision (DR-S11E04). Option B needs Authority & access at LIMITED or better — owners who'll approve quickly.

options.label: English only, until someone's free to translate
options.result: Spanish speakers wait for the busiest person in the room.
options.consequence: Leaves people out when it matters most.
options.fail: Access to warnings isn't optional; the accessibility lead owns how it's provided.

options.label: With Amara: qualified translators write templates for every standard warning; the director approves them in advance; the relay publishes the matching template with the same details; a live interpreter for briefings; captions carry the verbatim text
options.result: Eighteen templates approved on Friday. The interpreter joins every briefing from Monday.
options.consequence: Every language, prepared and approved before the storm.

options.label: Machine translation of the agency's verbatim text, with a disclaimer
options.result: Closer — and a machine still decides what ‘protect your life’ becomes.
options.consequence: The best you can do without approved templates — and still unchecked.

options.label: Imogen translates warnings herself
options.result: One more job for the person already writing the county's messages.
options.consequence: One busy person as the translator.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Relay an official warning in its owner’s words, with the agency’s name and time; add the county’s own guidance separately; only the director says “evacuate”. Time the chain (T = Σ steps) — and find the step that changed the meaning. Every language needs templates written by qualified translators and approved before the storm; captions carry the verbatim text. Nothing here is advice for a real emergency — follow your local officials.
REFLECTION (optional)  · When you pass on someone else’s words, where do you add your own?
